items.followUp: How many elements are present in the second and third periods of the periodic table?

rubric.description: Names the normal periods as the second and third periods.

rubric.why: States the defining number of elements in each normal period.
rubric.description: States that each contains eight elements.
rubric.how: Award for the correct number of elements.

modelAnswer: The second and third periods are considered normal periods.

items.followUp: Explain why atomic size generally decreases from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Identifies the increase in nuclear charge across a period.
rubric.description: Nuclear charge increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award for stating that nuclear charge increases.

rubric.why: Explains how the increased attraction affects atomic size.
rubric.description: The added electrons enter the same shell, so stronger attraction by the nucleus pulls them closer and decreases atomic size.
rubric.how: Award for linking the same shell and stronger nuclear attraction to the decrease in size.

modelAnswer: From left to right across a period, the nuclear charge increases.
The added electrons enter the same shell, so the stronger attraction between the nucleus and the electrons pulls them closer.
Therefore, the size of the atoms decreases.

items.followUp: Explain how two chlorine atoms form a covalent bond.

rubric.why: States how the atoms bond to one another.
rubric.description: More electronegative atoms can share electrons with each other.
rubric.how: Award for identifying sharing of electrons.

rubric.why: Names the resulting bond and supports the justification.
rubric.description: The shared electrons form a covalent bond; for example, two chlorine atoms form Cl₂.
rubric.how: Award for naming the covalent bond or giving the chlorine molecule example.

modelAnswer: When more electronegative atoms bond with each other, they share electrons rather than transfer them.
The shared electrons form a covalent bond; for example, two chlorine atoms form Cl₂.

items.followUp: Describe how magnesium and oxygen form an ionic bond.

rubric.description: A sodium atom loses one electron to form a sodium ion.
rubric.how: Award for stating that sodium loses one electron.

rubric.why: Identifies chlorine's electron gain and the resulting attraction.
rubric.description: A chlorine atom gains that electron; the oppositely charged ions attract to form an ionic bond.
rubric.how: Award for stating chlorine gains the electron and the ions attract, or for correctly naming the ionic bond formed.

modelAnswer: A sodium atom loses one electron to form a positively charged sodium ion, Na⁺.
A chlorine atom gains that electron to form a negatively charged chloride ion, Cl⁻.
The oppositely charged ions attract each other, forming an ionic bond.

items.followUp: Define a solute and give an example from a salt solution.

rubric.why: Defines the solvent by its role in dissolving another substance.
rubric.description: A solvent is the substance in which a solute dissolves.
Water is the solvent in a salt solution.
rubric.how: Award for correctly identifying water as the solvent in salt solution.

modelAnswer: A solvent is the substance in which a solute dissolves.
For example, water is the solvent in a salt solution.

items.followUp: What is the transition temperature of sulfur, and which change occurs at that temperature?

rubric.why: Defines the temperature by the change between forms.
rubric.description: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another.

rubric.why: Gives the standard sulfur example and temperature.
rubric.description: Rhombic sulfur changes into monoclinic sulfur at about 96°C.
rubric.how: Award for the correct sulfur forms and transition temperature.

modelAnswer: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotropic form of a substance changes into another.
For example, at about 96°C, rhombic sulfur changes into monoclinic sulfur.

items.followUp: State two differences between a colloid and a true solution.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the mixtures by their nature.
rubric.description: A solution is homogeneous, whereas a suspension is heterogeneous.
rubric.how: Award for correctly contrasting homogeneous and heterogeneous.

rubric.why: Gives a distinguishing property of suspensions.
rubric.description: Suspension particles settle on standing; solution particles do not settle.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing settling, with the comparison to a solution.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, whereas a suspension is heterogeneous.
The particles of a suspension settle on standing, whereas the particles of a solution do not settle.

items.followUp: What is the Tyndall effect, and how does it help identify a colloid?

rubric.why: Identifies the scattering responsible for the effect.
rubric.description: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light.
rubric.how: Award for stating that colloidal particles scatter light.

rubric.why: Describes the visible result of scattering.
rubric.description: Scattering makes the path of the light beam visible through the colloid.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the beam's path becomes visible.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles are large enough to scatter a beam of light passing through the colloid.
This scattering, called the Tyndall effect, makes the path of the light beam visible.
